title: Lucrece
html_source:
Lucrece, a legendary Roman housewife whose fate played a vital role in the transition from a Roman Kingdom into a Roman Republic. According to accounts from the Roman historian Livius and the Greek-Roman historian Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Lucretia’s suicide after her rape by an Etruscan king’s son was the immediate cause of the anti-monarchist rebellion that overthrew the monarchy.
The incident kindled the flames of dissatisfaction over the tyrannical methods of the last king of Rome, Lucius Tarquinius Superbus. As a result, the prominent families instituted a republic, drove the Royal Familyfrom Rome. Due to its sheer impact the rape itself became a major theme in European art and literature. Shakespeare penned a narrative poem entitled ‘The Rape of Lucrece’. He made allusion to this poem in some of his other work. He used this idea in Cymbeline (circa 1609–1610). In this play, Iachimo bets Posthumus (Imogen’s husband) that he can make Imogen commit adultery with him. He does not succeed. However, Iachimo convinces Posthumus otherwise using information about Imogen’s bedchamber and body. Iachimo hid in a trunk which was delivered to Imogen’s chamber under the pretence of safekeeping some jewels, a gift for her father, King Cymbeline. The scene in which he emerges from the trunk mimics the scene in The Rape of Lucrece. Indeed, Iachimo compares himself to Tarquin in the scene: “Our Tarquin thus, / Did softly press the rushes ere he waken’d / The chastity he wounded” (2.2.12–14).
